items.stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes reports three months of difficulty rising from chairs, dry mouth, and erectile dysfunction. Strength improves briefly after sustained effort. Examination shows proximal leg weakness and absent ankle reflexes. Which electrodiagnostic finding is most likely?
options: A decrement greater than ten percent with slow repetitive stimulation at rest only
Prolonged distal latencies with conduction block at common entrapment sites
Fibrillation potentials with long-duration, high-amplitude motor unit potentials
Marked increment after brief exercise or rapid stimulation
items.explanation: Proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, and areflexia that transiently improves with effort describe presynaptic calcium channel failure, as in Lambert-Eaton syndrome, often paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer. Presynaptic release rises with rapid stimulation, producing an increment. A slow-rate decrement alone fits postsynaptic myasthenia. Entrapment findings suggest a focal neuropathy, and denervation with large motor units suggests chronic neurogenic disease such as motor neuron loss.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl has daily episodes of brief staring with eyelid flutter and, in the past month, two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electroencephalography shows 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges. Which medication is the best choice?
options: Ethosuximide
Carbamazepine
Valproate
Phenytoin
items.explanation: Childhood absence epilepsy with added generalized tonic-clonic seizures needs a drug effective for both seizure types, and valproate (or lamotrigine) covers both. Ethosuximide controls absence seizures but does not protect against tonic-clonic events. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can aggravate absence seizures and generalized spike-and-wave activity. Lamotrigine is an acceptable alternative, though valproate is usually avoided in girls approaching childbearing years when other options work.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman taking an oral contraceptive has two weeks of worsening headache and then a focal seizure. MRI shows bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic infarcts. Which study is best to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: Conventional catheter angiography of the carotid arteries
Magnetic resonance venography
Transcranial Doppler of the basal arteries
Prolonged video electroencephalography
items.explanation: Headache, seizure, and bilateral parasagittal venous infarcts, especially with estrogen exposure, indicate cerebral venous thrombosis. Magnetic resonance venography or CT venography demonstrates the absent sinus flow. Arterial angiography and Doppler evaluate arterial disease, and electroencephalography records the seizure but does not explain its cause. Treatment is anticoagulation even when hemorrhagic infarction is present, and the seizure is managed with an appropriate antiseizure drug.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has dysarthria, a wing-beating tremor, and personality change. Slit-lamp examination shows golden-brown corneal rings. Which laboratory pattern is most likely?
options: Low serum ceruloplasmin with raised 24-hour urinary copper
High serum ceruloplasmin with low 24-hour urinary copper
Low serum ferritin with raised transferrin saturation
Normal ceruloplasmin with low serum copper and low urinary copper
items.explanation: Corneal Kayser-Fleischer rings with neuropsychiatric signs in a young adult indicate Wilson disease from ATP7B mutation. Biliary copper excretion fails, so ceruloplasmin is typically low and urinary copper is high. A high ceruloplasmin would argue against the disease. Iron indices point toward hemochromatosis or deficiency, and normal ceruloplasmin does not fit. Liver biopsy copper content and ATP7B genetic testing are confirmatory, and treatment with chelation or zinc should begin early.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has severe vomiting and hiccups for a week, followed by bilateral visual loss and a longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion spanning five vertebral segments. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody is positive. Which treatment should be avoided for long-term prevention?
options: Rituximab, an anti-CD20 antibody
Satralizumab, an interleukin-6 receptor blocker
Interferon beta
Inebilizumab, an anti-CD19 antibody
items.explanation: This is neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder with area postrema syndrome, optic neuritis, and longitudinally extensive myelitis. Interferon beta, effective in multiple sclerosis, can worsen relapses in this disease. Rituximab, satralizumab (an interleukin-6 receptor blocker), and inebilizumab (an anti-CD19 agent) are accepted maintenance therapies. Treatment choice therefore depends on antibody status, since fingolimod and natalizumab may also worsen neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.

items.stem: A 58-year-old former accountant has two years of disinhibited remarks, compulsive eating of sweets, loss of empathy, and apathy. Memory testing is relatively preserved. MRI shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. His brother had similar symptoms and developed motor neuron disease. Which gene is the most likely cause?
options: APOE epsilon 4 allele homozygosity
C9orf72 repeat expansion
PSEN1 missense mutation
PRNP octapeptide insertion
items.explanation: Early personality change, hyperorality, and frontotemporal atrophy define behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, and a family history of motor neuron disease points to a C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion, the most common genetic cause. APOE epsilon 4 is a risk factor for Alzheimer disease, PSEN1 causes early-onset Alzheimer disease, and PRNP mutations cause genetic prion disease with rapid decline.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has progressive hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI shows bilateral enhancing masses in both internal auditory canals and a spinal intradural extramedullary tumor. His father had similar tumors. Which gene is most likely affected?
options: NF1 on chromosome 17
TSC2 on chromosome 16
VHL on chromosome 3
NF2 on chromosome 22
items.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, with meningiomas or spinal tumors and an autosomal dominant family history, define neurofibromatosis type 2, caused by mutations in NF2 on chromosome 22 encoding merlin. NF1 causes cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, TSC2 causes tuberous sclerosis with cortical tubers, and VHL causes hemangioblastomas and renal tumors rather than bilateral acoustic tumors. Presymptomatic family testing and regular MRI surveillance are recommended, because early surgery or bevacizumab can help preserve hearing.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar disorder is mute, immobile, staring, and holds her arm in the air after it is lifted. She resists passive movement and has not eaten for two days. Vital signs are normal. Which treatment is the most appropriate first step?
options: Intravenous lorazepam
Haloperidol injection
Intravenous haloperidol with benztropine
Lithium dose increase
items.explanation: Mutism, stupor, posturing, and negativism define catatonia, and benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are first-line, with a rapid test dose often improving symptoms. Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Raising lithium does not treat the syndrome, and electroconvulsive therapy is used if lorazepam fails. Response is often seen within hours, and the underlying psychiatric or medical cause should then be addressed with continued dosing.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has had nightly attacks of severe right orbital pain lasting about 45 minutes for three weeks, with ipsilateral tearing, nasal congestion, and agitation. Oxygen helps acutely. Which preventive drug should be started for this cluster period, with electrocardiographic monitoring?
options: Propranolol
Amitriptyline
Sumatriptan daily
Verapamil
items.explanation: Strictly unilateral periorbital attacks with autonomic signs and restlessness define cluster headache. Verapamil is the preventive of choice, and because it can prolong the PR interval, an electrocardiogram is checked before and after dose increases. Propranolol and amitriptyline are not established for this indication, and daily triptan use risks medication overuse without preventing bouts. Short-term bridging with prednisone is an alternative, and high-flow oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan treats individual attacks.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has been punching and shouting during sleep for a year, once injuring his wife. Polysomnography shows REM sleep without atonia. He asks what this finding may predict. Which is the best answer?
options: A high chance of later developing narcolepsy with cataplexy
A benign finding with no long-term neurologic associations
A substantially higher risk of a later synucleinopathy
A future seizure disorder requiring antiseizure treatment
items.explanation: REM sleep behavior disorder confirmed by loss of REM atonia is a prodromal marker of alpha-synuclein disease, and most patients eventually develop Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or multiple system atrophy. It is not linked to narcolepsy risk and is not a benign variant. Treatment includes bedroom safety, melatonin, or clonazepam with caution. Counseling should also cover bedroom safety, since injury to the patient or partner is the immediate concern.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman taking a thiazide diuretic is confused after a week of vomiting. Serum sodium is 105 mmol per liter and she is hypovolemic. Isotonic saline is started and her urine output increases sharply. What is the main goal to avoid osmotic demyelination?
options: Correct the serum sodium fully to normal within the first six hours of treatment
Limit the sodium rise to 8 mmol per liter or less in 24 hours
Give isotonic saline at the same rate until symptoms resolve completely
Check the sodium only once daily until the patient is fully alert
items.explanation: In chronic severe hyponatremia, rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination, with dysarthria, quadriparesis, and locked-in features days later. Risk is high with hypokalemia and malnutrition, and brisk water diuresis after volume repletion can overshoot. Limit correction to about 8 mmol per liter daily, check sodium every few hours, and be prepared to relower with desmopressin.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has fever, neck stiffness, and a depressed level of consciousness. Lumbar puncture shows 1,800 neutrophils per microliter, low glucose, and high protein. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate in addition to dexamethasone?
options: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin
Ceftriaxone alone given at high intravenous dose
Acyclovir alone pending viral PCR results
Vancomycin and metronidazole for anaerobic coverage
items.explanation: Bacterial meningitis in an adult over 50 is treated empirically with vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin plus ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes, with dexamethasone started before or with the first antibiotic dose. Ceftriaxone alone leaves Listeria and resistant pneumococcus uncovered, acyclovir targets herpes viruses, and metronidazole does not provide meningeal coverage. Dexamethasone reduces neurologic sequelae mainly in pneumococcal disease, and therapy is adjusted once culture and susceptibility results return.

items.stem: A 17-year-old cyclist is hit on the left temple, is briefly unconscious, then talks normally for two hours before becoming drowsy with a dilated left pupil. CT shows a biconvex hyperdense extraaxial collection. What is the best management?
options: Observation with repeat CT in 24 hours
Emergency surgical evacuation
Mannitol alone and discharge
Lumbar puncture to measure pressure
items.explanation: A lucid interval followed by decline and a blown pupil, with a lens-shaped collection from tear of the middle meningeal artery, indicates epidural hematoma with herniation. Prompt evacuation is life-saving and outcome is excellent when done early. Observation is unsafe, osmotherapy only bridges, and lumbar puncture risks fatal herniation. Delay causes uncal herniation and death, so imaging that shows a hematoma with mass effect leads directly to the operating room.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with hypertension has two days of constant vertigo, nausea, and inability to walk unaided. Gaze evoked nystagmus changes direction with the direction of gaze, the head impulse test is normal bilaterally, and there is a skew deviation. What is the best interpretation?
options: Vestibular neuritis involving the vestibular nerve and ganglion
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the posterior canal
Meniere disease with endolymphatic hydrops
A central cause such as brainstem or cerebellar infarction
items.explanation: In acute continuous vertigo, a normal head impulse test, direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, or skew deviation, the three components of the HINTS examination, indicates a central lesion. Vestibular neuritis shows a corrective saccade on head impulse and unidirectional nystagmus. Positional vertigo is brief and triggered by movement, and Meniere disease is episodic with hearing loss. Bedside testing therefore guides urgent MRI and stroke management, since early CT often misses posterior fossa infarction.

items.stem: A 61-year-old immunocompetent man has subacute confusion. MRI shows a solitary homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with restricted diffusion crossing the corpus callosum. He has not received corticosteroids. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate high-dose dexamethasone to shrink the lesion
Empiric whole-brain radiation without a tissue diagnosis
Stereotactic biopsy, withholding corticosteroids if safe
Resection of the mass with the aim of cure
items.explanation: A homogeneously enhancing periventricular lesion with restricted diffusion suggests primary central nervous system lymphoma. Steroids can cause the tumor to shrink or vanish and render the biopsy nondiagnostic, so they are held if the patient is stable. Empiric radiation without tissue is inappropriate, and extensive resection offers no survival advantage for this chemosensitive tumor. Methotrexate-based chemotherapy is the cornerstone of treatment after diagnosis, with radiation used selectively because of delayed neurotoxicity.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man is stabbed in the left posterior chest at the T8 level. Examination shows left leg weakness with hyperreflexia, loss of vibration and position sense in the left leg, and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the right leg below the umbilicus. Which lesion best explains these findings?
options: Left spinal cord hemisection
Right spinal cord hemisection at the same level
Central cord syndrome from hyperextension injury
Anterior spinal artery infarction of the lower thoracic cord
items.explanation: Ipsilateral weakness and loss of dorsal column function with contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion define Brown-Sequard syndrome. Corticospinal and dorsal column fibers are uncrossed in the cord, while spinothalamic fibers cross within a segment or two of entry. A right lesion would reverse the pattern, central cord syndrome spares the legs relatively, and anterior cord infarction spares position sense.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has weeks of brief arm and face jerks many times daily, then amnesia and confusion. Sodium is 125 mmol per liter, and MRI shows right mesial temporal hyperintensity. Serum antibodies against LGI1 are positive. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Antiseizure drugs alone, because the seizures respond well
High-dose corticosteroids with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
Thymectomy followed by pyridostigmine
Observation until the antibody titer rises further
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatremia, and limbic encephalitis with LGI1 antibodies describe autoimmune encephalitis in which early immunotherapy prevents cognitive injury. First-line treatment is corticosteroids with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange. The seizures respond poorly to antiseizure drugs alone, thymectomy is for myasthenia, and waiting risks permanent memory loss. Tumor screening is also performed, though association is less frequent than with other antibodies.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with Parkinson disease has dizziness on standing, with a drop in blood pressure from 140/80 to 100/60 mm Hg after 3 minutes upright and no rise in heart rate. After nonpharmacologic measures fail, which drug is most appropriate?
options: Propranolol
Amlodipine
Midodrine
Tamsulosin
items.explanation: A sustained fall in systolic pressure of 20 mm Hg or more without a compensatory heart rate rise indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. After fluids, salt, compression garments, and head-up sleeping, midodrine or droxidopa or fludrocortisone can be used, with attention to supine hypertension. Propranolol and amlodipine lower blood pressure and heart rate response. Tamsulosin is an alpha blocker that lowers standing pressure further.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy has had high arches, frequent ankle sprains, and slowly progressive foot drop since early childhood. His father has similar features. Nerve conduction studies show uniform slowing of motor conduction velocities to about 20 m/s in all nerves. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: Duplication of PMP22
Deletion of PMP22 on the same chromosome
Point mutation in MFN2 affecting mitochondrial fusion
Trinucleotide expansion in the frataxin gene
items.explanation: A childhood onset length-dependent neuropathy with uniform demyelinating slowing below 38 m/s is typical of Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, caused by PMP22 duplication. A PMP22 deletion produces hereditary neuropathy with pressure palsies, with episodic focal palsies and non-uniform slowing. MFN2 mutations cause axonal disease with near-normal velocities, and frataxin expansion causes Friedreich ataxia with sensory axonal loss.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a generalized convulsion lasting 12 minutes. Intramuscular midazolam was given 10 minutes ago and he is still seizing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Intravenous pentobarbital infusion with intubation
Oral lamotrigine loading through a nasogastric tube
Intravenous haloperidol to reduce agitation
Intravenous levetiracetam loading dose
items.explanation: Benzodiazepine failure defines established status epilepticus, and an intravenous second-line agent should follow immediately. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate performed similarly in a randomized trial. Anesthetic coma with pentobarbital is third line, reserved for refractory status. Oral drugs are too slow, and haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold. Doses should be adequate and given promptly, because delayed treatment lowers the chance that the seizure will stop and increases neuronal injury.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman arrives two hours after sudden left hemiparesis and aphasia. Blood pressure is 190/105 mm Hg, glucose is normal, and CT shows no hemorrhage. She meets every other criterion for thrombolysis. What is the best management?
options: Withhold thrombolysis permanently because the pressure was elevated
Give alteplase now and treat the pressure afterward
Lower pressure below 185/110 mm Hg, then give alteplase
Give aspirin and recheck in 24 hours before deciding
items.explanation: Pressure above 185/110 mm Hg is a correctable contraindication: it should be reduced with an agent such as labetalol or nicardipine and maintained below that threshold, after which thrombolysis proceeds. Giving the drug before control raises hemorrhage risk. Withholding it forever or substituting aspirin wastes the narrow time window. Alteplase or tenecteplase can then be given within the standard window of up to four and a half hours from onset, with close monitoring afterward.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for six years. She now has repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and finger movements that distress her. Her psychiatric symptoms are stable. Which agent is the best addition?
options: Benztropine
Increased risperidone dose
Propranolol
Valbenazine
items.explanation: Persistent orofacial and limb movements after long dopamine blocker exposure define tardive dyskinesia. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine reduce it. Anticholinergics like benztropine can worsen tardive dyskinesia, a higher antipsychotic dose masks but worsens the underlying process, and propranolol treats akathisia. Dose reduction or switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic such as clozapine may also be considered when psychiatric control allows.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has received natalizumab for three years for relapsing multiple sclerosis and is positive for JC virus antibody. Over three weeks she develops left hemiparesis and visual neglect. MRI shows a large T2 hyperintense subcortical lesion involving U-fibers with no enhancement or mass effect. Which test is most useful to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: JC virus PCR on cerebrospinal fluid
Repeat serum JC virus antibody index
Aquaporin-4 antibody in serum
Brain biopsy for tumefactive demyelination
items.explanation: Progressive focal deficits with a nonenhancing subcortical lesion in a natalizumab-treated, JC virus-seropositive patient indicate progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR confirms it. A serum antibody only shows exposure, not active infection. Aquaporin-4 antibody addresses neuromyelitis optica, and biopsy is reserved for cases where noninvasive testing is unrevealing. Early diagnosis matters because stopping natalizumab, with plasma exchange to remove drug and monitoring for immune reconstitution, is the central management step.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has two years of word-finding pauses and difficulty repeating long sentences. Single-word comprehension, grammar, and motor speech are intact. MRI shows left posterior temporal and inferior parietal atrophy. Which underlying pathology is most likely?
options: TDP-43 type C proteinopathy in the temporal lobe
Alzheimer disease pathology
Four-repeat tauopathy with astrocytic plaques
Prion protein accumulation with spongiform change
items.explanation: Slowed speech with anomia and impaired sentence repetition, but preserved grammar and single-word comprehension, defines logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia, which most often reflects Alzheimer pathology and may be confirmed with amyloid biomarkers. TDP-43 type C is typical of semantic variant, and four-repeat tau is linked to nonfluent variant. Prion disease progresses much faster. Cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and tau profiles or amyloid PET can support this pathology during life when the clinical picture is atypical.

items.stem: A term newborn has a five-minute Apgar score of 3 after a placental abruption and develops seizures and hypotonia at three hours of age. Cord arterial pH is 6.9. Which intervention within the first six hours has the best evidence of improving outcome?
options: High-dose phenobarbital given prophylactically to all infants
Intravenous dexamethasone given to reduce cerebral edema early
Controlled whole-body or head cooling for 72 hours
Hyperventilation to a low carbon dioxide level for 24 hours
items.explanation: Moderate to severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy in a term infant is treated with therapeutic hypothermia started within six hours of birth, which lowers death and disability. Prophylactic barbiturates and steroids lack proven benefit, and hyperventilation reduces cerebral blood flow and can worsen injury in a vulnerable brain. Eligibility requires a gestational age of at least 36 weeks and evidence of acidosis, or a low Apgar score with encephalopathy.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has weakness of the right leg after a stressful event. Hip extension is weak on testing but returns to full strength when she flexes the left hip against resistance. Reflexes and imaging are normal. What is the best initial management approach?
options: Explain the diagnosis positively and refer for specialized physiotherapy
Order repeated advanced imaging until the family is fully reassured about it
Tell her the symptoms are imagined and discharge her without follow-up
Start long-term benzodiazepine therapy to relieve anxiety and weakness
items.explanation: A positive Hoover sign, with weakness that resolves during contralateral effort, supports functional neurological disorder based on positive signs. Treatment starts with a clear, nonjudgmental explanation followed by physiotherapy and, where needed, psychotherapy. Repeated testing reinforces illness fears, dismissal harms trust, and benzodiazepines add dependence risk without benefit. Recovery depends on engagement with rehabilitation, so reassurance that the symptoms are real and potentially reversible improves outcomes.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, and one episode of transient blurred vision. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 92 mm per hour. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for biopsy results before giving any corticosteroid
Start prednisone now and arrange temporal artery biopsy
Begin a triptan and reassess in one week as an outpatient
Order lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure first
items.explanation: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms threatens permanent blindness, so corticosteroids are started immediately without waiting for pathology, and biopsy is performed soon after because histology stays informative for days to weeks. Delaying treatment risks vision loss, a triptan treats migraine, and lumbar puncture does not address arterial inflammation. Visual loss in this condition is often permanent once established, which is why therapy is never postponed for diagnostic confirmation.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has excessive daytime sleepiness for two years and falls to the floor with brief loss of muscle tone when she laughs. After two weeks of stopping stimulants, a multiple sleep latency test follows a normal overnight study. Which result best supports her diagnosis?
options: Mean sleep latency of fifteen minutes with no sleep-onset REM periods recorded
Apnea-hypopnea index of 25 events per hour on the preceding night
Periodic limb movement index of 40 per hour on the preceding night
Mean latency of eight minutes or less with two sleep-onset REM periods
items.explanation: Sleepiness with emotion-triggered cataplexy suggests narcolepsy type 1. Confirmation relies on a short mean sleep latency and at least two sleep-onset REM periods after a night free of other sleep disorder, with low cerebrospinal hypocretin as an alternative. Normal latency excludes pathologic sleepiness, and an elevated apnea or limb movement index describes other disorders. Hypocretin deficiency in cerebrospinal fluid is the biological basis, and sodium oxybate treats both sleepiness and cataplexy.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks of pregnancy has persistent vomiting for six weeks and now has confusion, horizontal nystagmus, and a wide-based gait. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Intravenous glucose alone to correct the metabolic state
Oral multivitamin taken with meals every morning
Intravenous thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids
Intravenous haloperidol to control agitation and confusion
items.explanation: Confusion, ocular signs, and ataxia after prolonged vomiting indicate Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. Thiamine is given parenterally at once and before glucose, since carbohydrate loading can precipitate or worsen the syndrome. An oral multivitamin is inadequate, glucose alone can aggravate the deficit, and antipsychotics do not treat the cause. Dosing continues for several days at a high parenteral dose, and magnesium is replaced because thiamine requires it as a cofactor.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has three days of fever, behavioral change, and a focal seizure. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the left medial temporal lobe and insula. Cerebrospinal fluid has 60 lymphocytes and 150 red cells per microliter. What is the best next step in management?
options: Wait for the PCR result before starting any antiviral treatment
Start high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone as monotherapy first
Begin an antiseizure drug and observe her over 24 hours
Start intravenous acyclovir now and send herpes simplex virus PCR
items.explanation: Fever, behavior change, seizures, and temporal lobe involvement suggest herpes simplex virus encephalitis, which has high mortality when untreated. Acyclovir is started empirically without waiting for PCR, since early therapy determines outcome. Steroids alone are not antiviral, and seizure control alone ignores the infectious cause. Herpes simplex virus PCR on cerebrospinal fluid is highly sensitive but can be falsely negative within the first 72 hours, so treatment continues.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man falls from a ladder and has immediate bilateral arm weakness greater than leg weakness, with burning in the hands and preserved vibration and position sense. Cervical MRI shows hyperextension injury with cord edema and no fracture. Which syndrome is this?
options: Central cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Sequard syndrome
Posterior cord syndrome
items.explanation: Hyperextension injury with disproportionate upper limb weakness, sensory loss over the hands, and preserved posterior column function describes central cord syndrome, caused by damage to the medial corticospinal fibers serving the arms. Anterior cord syndrome causes loss of motor and pain function with preserved vibration. Brown-Sequard shows ipsilateral weakness with contralateral pain loss. Posterior cord syndrome affects proprioception with preserved strength.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has sudden diplopia worse at distance, with the left eye turned inward and unable to abduct. Pupils and the rest of the neurologic examination are normal. She has hypertension and diabetes. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Compressive posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Microvascular ischemic abducens nerve palsy
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia from demyelination
Myasthenia gravis with ocular involvement only
items.explanation: An isolated abducens palsy in an older patient with vascular risk factors is usually microvascular and improves over weeks to months. Posterior communicating aneurysm causes a pupil-involving third nerve palsy. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia produces impaired adduction with abducting nystagmus, not failed abduction. Myasthenia causes variable, fatigable diplopia with ptosis and does not usually present as a fixed single nerve palsy.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has 3 weeks of headache, progressive left leg weakness, and a ring-enhancing mass with surrounding edema in the right frontal lobe. She has a known history of lung cancer. After starting dexamethasone, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Full brain MRI to count lesions before local therapy
Whole brain radiation therapy only without further imaging
Empiric antibiotics for a brain abscess for 6 weeks
Prophylactic levetiracetam for all patients without seizures
items.explanation: A new enhancing mass in a patient with known systemic cancer is most likely a metastasis, and dexamethasone reduces vasogenic edema. Contrast MRI of the whole brain defines the number of lesions and guides surgery or stereotactic radiosurgery. Radiation planning without full imaging is premature. Antibiotics are not indicated without infection signs. Antiseizure drugs are not recommended prophylactically in patients who have not had a seizure.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a tumor invading the anterior temporal lobe that interrupts fibers sweeping forward around the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. Which visual field defect is expected?
options: Ipsilateral inferior quadrantanopia
Contralateral superior quadrantanopia
Contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia
Bitemporal hemianopia
items.explanation: Fibers carrying the inferior retina, which represents the upper visual field, loop forward through the temporal lobe as Meyer loop. Damage there produces a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, often called pie in the sky. Parietal lesions affecting the upper optic radiation give contralateral inferior quadrantanopia, while chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia. Optic radiation lesions never produce an ipsilateral defect.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has 2 weeks of psychosis, memory loss, orofacial dyskinesias, and a generalized seizure. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. Pelvic ultrasound shows an ovarian teratoma. Which antibody is most likely present?
options: Anti-Hu antibody in the serum and CSF
Anti-GAD65 antibody at low titer
Anti-Ma2 antibody in the serum
Anti-NMDA receptor antibody in CSF
items.explanation: Psychiatric symptoms followed by seizures, dyskinesias, and autonomic instability in a young woman with an ovarian teratoma is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, best confirmed by cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing, with tumor removal and immunotherapy. Anti-Hu causes sensory neuronopathy and limbic encephalitis with small cell cancer. Low-titer GAD65 is not specific. Anti-Ma2 is linked with testicular tumors and brainstem or diencephalic disease.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with well-controlled generalized myasthenia gravis is treated for a urinary tract infection. Two days later she develops ptosis, dysphagia, and shortness of breath. Which antibiotic was most likely prescribed?
options: Cephalexin
Nitrofurantoin
Ciprofloxacin
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
items.explanation: Fluoroquinolones can impair neuromuscular transmission and carry a boxed warning for worsening myasthenia gravis, sometimes causing crisis. Aminoglycosides and macrolides are also risky. Cephalexin, nitrofurantoin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are not established exacerbating agents at the neuromuscular junction; nitrofurantoin is better known for a length-dependent neuropathy with prolonged use. Infections themselves can also trigger crisis, so early treatment and careful antibiotic selection both matter in patients with myasthenia.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy takes valproate and plans to become pregnant. She has been seizure-free for three years. What is the best advice?
options: Change to lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception
Continue valproate and add high-dose folic acid alone
Stop all antiseizure medication as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Change to topiramate for its lower malformation risk
items.explanation: Valproate carries the highest risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental impairment, so women of childbearing potential should be moved to safer agents such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception, since a switch during pregnancy is less effective. Folic acid does not remove the risk. Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures, and topiramate has its own oral cleft risk.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man is found with right hemiparesis and gaze deviation 14 hours after he was last seen normal. CT angiography shows a left M1 occlusion, and perfusion imaging shows a small core with a large penumbra. What is the best treatment?
options: Supportive care only because the 6-hour window has passed
Intravenous thrombolysis alone with no vascular procedure
Endovascular thrombectomy based on imaging selection
Emergency decompressive craniectomy
items.explanation: Late-window trials selected patients by clinical deficit and perfusion mismatch and showed clear benefit from thrombectomy up to 24 hours after last known well. Time alone does not exclude him. Thrombolysis alone is outside its time window and rarely opens a proximal occlusion, and craniectomy is for malignant edema after large infarction. Selection by imaging rather than the clock allows treatment in carefully screened patients between six and twenty-four hours after onset.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has a bilateral postural hand tremor that interferes with holding a cup and began in her fifties. Her mother had similar tremor. She has moderate asthma. Which medication is the most appropriate first-line choice?
options: Propranolol
Primidone
Levodopa
Trihexyphenidyl
items.explanation: Familial postural and kinetic tremor without rest tremor or bradykinesia is essential tremor. Propranolol and primidone are first line, but nonselective beta blockers can precipitate bronchospasm, so primidone is preferred with asthma. Levodopa treats Parkinson disease, and anticholinergics are poorly tolerated in older adults and are not first-line for this tremor. Focused ultrasound or deep brain stimulation is considered when medications fail or cause intolerable adverse effects in disabling tremor.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy has fever, drowsiness, and bilateral visual blurring ten days after a viral illness. MRI shows large, poorly marginated T2 lesions in both thalami and the pons, and examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling. Serum testing is most likely to identify which antibody?
options: Aquaporin-4 IgG in serum
NMDA receptor IgG in cerebrospinal fluid
Glial fibrillary acidic protein IgG in cerebrospinal fluid
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG
items.explanation: A child with encephalopathy, optic neuritis, and large fluffy lesions after infection fits acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody is common in this presentation, often with a monophasic course. Aquaporin-4 antibody is rare in young children, NMDA receptor antibody causes psychiatric and movement symptoms without these lesions, and GFAP antibody produces meningoencephalomyelitis with radial perivascular enhancement.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with early Alzheimer disease and two copies of the apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 allele is considered for an anti-amyloid antibody. What is the most important safety measure?
options: Serial MRI for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities
Annual echocardiography to look for valvular heart disease
Weekly serum ammonia levels to detect hepatic toxicity
Baseline and monthly nerve conduction studies for neuropathy
items.explanation: Anti-amyloid antibodies such as lecanemab cause amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or microhemorrhage, and the risk is highest in epsilon 4 homozygotes, who may also develop symptomatic events. Scheduled MRI before early infusions detects them, and antithrombotic use warrants caution. Cardiac, hepatic, and nerve toxicity are not characteristic of these agents. Hence a baseline MRI and further scans before specific infusions are standard, with dosing paused if abnormalities appear.

items.stem: A 20-month-old girl who walked at 13 months has lost purposeful hand use, wrings her hands continuously, and has lost her few words. She also has breath-holding spells and slowed head growth. Which gene is most likely mutated?
options: CDKL5 mutation
SMN1 deletion
FMR1 CGG expansion
MECP2 mutation
items.explanation: Regression after initially normal development, stereotyped hand wringing, loss of language, and deceleration of head growth in a girl describe Rett syndrome, caused by mutations in the X-linked gene MECP2. CDKL5 causes an early refractory epilepsy phenotype, SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy with weakness, and FMR1 expansions cause fragile X syndrome. Seizures, scoliosis, and gait abnormality commonly emerge later in the course, so supportive therapy proceeds alongside genetic counseling.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has sudden, uncontrollable episodes of crying and laughing that are out of proportion to her mood and last under a minute. She denies sadness. Which treatment is approved for this condition?
options: Haloperidol given at a low daily dose for agitation
Dextromethorphan combined with quinidine
Modafinil given in the morning for daytime fatigue
Baclofen titrated upward for spasticity and spasms
items.explanation: Involuntary, exaggerated emotional expression that does not match the underlying mood describes pseudobulbar affect, seen in multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and stroke. Dextromethorphan with quinidine reduces episodes. Haloperidol adds sedation and movement side effects, modafinil addresses fatigue, and baclofen treats spasticity without altering emotional lability. Common adverse effects include dizziness and diarrhea, and an electrocardiogram is advised because of the quinidine component in vulnerable patients.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with obesity has daily headaches worse when lying down, pulsatile tinnitus, and brief visual obscurations. Examination shows bilateral papilledema, and MRI with venography is normal. Opening pressure is 38 cm of water with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. Which management is most appropriate initially?
options: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement as first treatment
Optic nerve sheath fenestration for every patient at diagnosis
Acetazolamide with a structured weight loss program
Long-term dexamethasone to lower cerebrospinal fluid pressure
items.explanation: Papilledema with elevated pressure, normal imaging, and normal fluid is idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Weight loss and acetazolamide are first-line, and vision is monitored with perimetry. Shunting and optic nerve sheath fenestration are reserved for progressive or severe visual loss despite medical therapy, and steroids are avoided because they promote weight gain and rebound. Acetazolamide works by reducing cerebrospinal fluid production, and serial visual field testing guides follow-up and escalation.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with obesity reports loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and excessive daytime sleepiness. In-laboratory polysomnography shows 38 obstructive events per hour with oxygen desaturation. He cannot tolerate positive airway pressure masks. Which alternative has the best evidence for selected patients?
options: Oral modafinil alone as definitive therapy
Hypoglossal nerve stimulation
Zolpidem at bedtime to deepen sleep
Sodium oxybate at bedtime
items.explanation: Moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea treatment relies on positive airway pressure, with hypoglossal nerve stimulation approved for selected patients with limited body mass index and no concentric palatal collapse. Modafinil may reduce sleepiness but leaves the airway unprotected. Sedative hypnotics can worsen obstructive events. Sodium oxybate can depress respiration and is contraindicated in untreated sleep apnea.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a history of gastric bypass 10 years ago has 3 months of tingling feet, gait unsteadiness, and fatigue. Examination shows loss of vibration and position sense and brisk knee reflexes. Hemoglobin is low with macrocytosis. What is the most likely cause?
options: Vitamin B6 toxicity from supplements
Copper excess from supplements
Vitamin B12 deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency with rickets
items.explanation: Macrocytic anemia with posterior column loss and upper motor neuron signs indicates subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency, common after bariatric surgery because intrinsic factor and absorption are impaired. Excess vitamin B6 causes a sensory neuronopathy without macrocytosis. Copper deficiency, not excess, produces a similar myeloneuropathy. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone and muscle weakness rather than posterior column degeneration.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has 2 days of fever, personality change, and a new focal seizure. Magnetic resonance imaging shows hyperintensity in the left medial temporal lobe. While awaiting cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction results, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Start intravenous acyclovir immediately
Wait for polymerase chain reaction confirmation
Begin oral valacyclovir at home
Give intravenous ganciclovir
items.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis has high mortality and morbidity when treatment is delayed, so empiric intravenous acyclovir begins as soon as it is suspected and continues for 14 to 21 days if confirmed. Waiting for confirmation risks irreversible damage. Oral valacyclovir does not achieve adequate central nervous system levels for encephalitis, and ganciclovir is used for cytomegalovirus, not first-line herpes simplex.

items.stem: A 19-year-old football player has a concussion with headache and dizziness. Symptoms resolved after 5 days of relative rest. What is the recommended approach to return to play?
options: Immediate return once the player feels well on the sideline
Strict dark-room rest for 2 weeks before any activity
Return to contact practice on the same day as light jogging
Graded stepwise return after symptom resolution
items.explanation: Current consensus favors brief rest followed by a graded, symptom-limited return to activity, with progression only if symptoms do not recur and with clinician clearance before contact play. Same-day return risks a second injury during a vulnerable period. Prolonged strict rest has not been shown to help and may delay recovery. Skipping steps to contact practice ignores the gradual protocol meant to detect recurrent symptoms.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has brief spinning vertigo lasting under a minute when she turns over in bed or looks up. A Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right causes upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short delay that fatigues. What is the best treatment?
options: The Epley canalith repositioning maneuver
Long-term meclizine as the primary treatment
Intratympanic gentamicin injection
Brain MRI followed by vestibular suppressant therapy
items.explanation: Brief positional vertigo with a latent, fatiguing upbeating torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike is posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, treated at the bedside with canalith repositioning. Vestibular suppressants such as meclizine are not recommended because they do not clear the canal debris. Gentamicin is reserved for Meniere disease refractory to therapy. Imaging is not needed when the history and maneuver are typical.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has eight months of progressive right hand weakness and cramps, tongue fasciculations, brisk jaw jerk, and hyperreflexia in the legs. Electromyography shows widespread denervation in cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions. Which treatment has been shown to modestly prolong survival?
options: Coenzyme Q10
High-dose vitamin E
Minocycline
Riluzole
items.explanation: The mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs with denervation in three regions meet criteria for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Riluzole, a glutamate release inhibitor, prolongs survival by a few months. Coenzyme Q10, vitamin E, and minocycline were studied in randomized trials and showed no benefit, and minocycline was possibly harmful in one trial. Edaravone and tofersen are further options in selected patients.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has focal impaired-awareness seizures despite adequate trials of levetiracetam and then lamotrigine. MRI shows right hippocampal sclerosis concordant with his EEG and seizure semiology. What is the best next step?
options: A third antiseizure medication as monotherapy
Implantation of a vagus nerve stimulator
Presurgical evaluation at an epilepsy center
A trial of the ketogenic diet
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy, and the chance of freedom with a third drug is small. Concordant mesial temporal sclerosis makes him an excellent surgical candidate, and temporal lobectomy outperforms continued medication in randomized trials. Neurostimulation and diet are palliative options for nonresectable cases. Surgical candidacy should be assessed early, since patients are often referred years later than guidelines advise after failing two medications.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man taking warfarin has sudden headache and left hemiparesis. CT shows a deep right basal ganglia hemorrhage, and his INR is 3.8. Which reversal strategy is most appropriate?
options: Fresh frozen plasma alone infused slowly over several hours
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K
Platelet transfusion combined with desmopressin infusion now
Intravenous tranexamic acid as the sole reversal agent used
items.explanation: Warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage needs rapid correction of the INR. Prothrombin complex concentrate works in minutes without the large volume of plasma, and vitamin K sustains the effect after the factors wear off. Plasma alone is slow and volume-limited. Platelets are used for antiplatelet effects, and tranexamic acid alone does not reverse a vitamin K antagonist.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has rigidity, bradykinesia, and seizures. His father developed chorea at age 40, and his grandmother had late-onset disease. Which genetic mechanism best explains the early onset?
options: Expansion of the CAG repeat during maternal transmission
Loss of the maternal allele at the imprinted locus on chromosome 15
Expansion of the CAG repeat during paternal transmission
Acquired somatic mutation in striatal neurons
items.explanation: Huntington disease is caused by CAG expansion in HTT, and anticipation is most marked with paternal transmission because repeats expand in spermatogenesis. Large expansions cause juvenile onset, the Westphal variant with rigidity and seizures. Maternal transmission shows less instability, imprinting loss describes Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes, and acquired somatic mutation does not explain a family pattern.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has stable relapsing multiple sclerosis and is delivering her first child next month. She asks when her risk of relapse will be highest. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Relapse risk is highest during the third trimester of pregnancy and falls after delivery.
Relapse risk falls in late pregnancy and rises in the first three months postpartum.
Pregnancy permanently worsens long-term disability and should be avoided in all patients.
Breastfeeding invariably triggers relapses in the months after delivery in most patients.
items.explanation: Relapse rates decline across pregnancy, especially in the third trimester, then rebound during the first three months postpartum before returning to baseline. Long-term disability is not worsened by pregnancy. Exclusive breastfeeding may be associated with a lower postpartum relapse rate, so it is not a trigger. Counseling should address resuming disease-modifying therapy compatible with her feeding plan.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations of children in the house, and acting out his dreams. After a single dose of haloperidol in the emergency department he became rigid and unresponsive. Which treatment is the best first choice for his distressing hallucinations?
options: Rivastigmine
Haloperidol at a lower dose
Olanzapine
Benztropine
items.explanation: Fluctuations, visual hallucinations, and dream enactment suggest dementia with Lewy bodies, in which dopamine blockers can cause severe sensitivity reactions. A cholinesterase inhibitor such as rivastigmine often reduces hallucinations. Reducing the haloperidol dose does not remove the risk, olanzapine is also poorly tolerated, and anticholinergics worsen cognition and psychosis. Quetiapine at low dose is a second option if hallucinations persist despite a cholinesterase inhibitor.

items.stem: A newborn has a unilateral facial capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid. At six months of age she has a focal seizure. Which additional finding should be screened for urgently?
options: Cardiac rhabdomyoma on echocardiography
Renal angiomyolipoma on ultrasonography
Optic pathway glioma on MRI
Glaucoma on ophthalmologic examination
items.explanation: A capillary malformation in the ophthalmic trigeminal distribution with seizures suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome, with leptomeningeal angiomatosis and a somatic GNAQ mutation. Choroidal involvement causes glaucoma, so early eye assessment protects vision. Rhabdomyoma and angiomyolipoma belong to tuberous sclerosis, and optic glioma belongs to neurofibromatosis type 1. Early seizure control and regular intraocular pressure measurement matter, since both affect long-term neurologic and visual outcomes.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man reports 6 weeks of persistent worry about many everyday matters, muscle tension, poor sleep, and irritability, present most days, without panic attacks or low mood. He asks about a first-line medication that does not cause dependence. Which agent is most appropriate?
options: Alprazolam as needed
Escitalopram
Quetiapine at bedtime
Bupropion extended release
items.explanation: Excessive, hard-to-control worry with tension and insomnia for at least 6 months defines generalized anxiety disorder, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are first-line. Alprazolam works quickly but risks tolerance and dependence, so it is not preferred for long-term treatment. Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic with metabolic risk and limited first-line role. Bupropion lacks reliable anxiolytic benefit and may worsen anxiety.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has 3 weeks of severe, strictly right periorbital pain lasting about 60 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day, with ipsilateral tearing, nasal congestion, and restlessness. Which is the most effective acute treatment?
options: Oral sumatriptan 100 mg at onset
Oral acetaminophen 1,000 mg tablets
Intramuscular ketorolac injection
High-flow oxygen by mask
items.explanation: Short severe unilateral periorbital attacks with autonomic features and restlessness define cluster headache. Inhaled oxygen at 12 to 15 liters per minute and subcutaneous or intranasal triptans abort attacks quickly. Oral triptans act too slowly because the attacks peak within minutes. Acetaminophen and ketorolac are too weak or slow for this pain and are not recommended for cluster attacks.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has had daily irresistible sleep attacks for 2 years, brief loss of muscle tone when laughing, vivid hallucinations on falling asleep, and episodes of paralysis on waking. A multiple sleep latency test is planned. Which finding supports the diagnosis?
options: Mean sleep latency of 14 minutes with no REM periods
Five or more obstructive apneas per hour on the preceding night
Latency 8 minutes or less and two REM onsets
Periodic limb movements index above 15 per hour
items.explanation: Cataplexy with sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations indicates narcolepsy type 1. The multiple sleep latency test shows a mean latency of 8 minutes or less and at least two sleep-onset REM periods, and a REM period on the preceding polysomnogram counts toward the total. A long latency without REM argues against it. Obstructive apnea and limb movements can cause sleepiness but do not explain cataplexy.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with chronic malnutrition after prolonged vomiting develops confusion, nystagmus, and a wide-based gait. Glucose is normal. Which is the correct order of treatment?
options: Intravenous thiamine before any glucose-containing fluids
Intravenous glucose first, with thiamine given after recovery
Oral folate alone until the gait improves
Intravenous magnesium alone for 48 hours
items.explanation: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, and ataxia suggest Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. Parenteral thiamine must be given promptly and before or with glucose, because glucose can precipitate or worsen the crisis in a depleted patient. Folate does not treat it. Magnesium is a cofactor and is often replaced too, but it is not the treatment alone and does not replace thiamine.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has frequent falls and uses his hands to push up on his thighs when rising from the floor. He has enlarged calves and a serum creatine kinase of 22,000 U/L. What is the best next diagnostic test?
options: Needle electromyography of the proximal leg muscles bilaterally
Open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps with dystrophin staining
Deletion analysis of the SMN1 gene with copy number testing
Deletion and duplication analysis of the dystrophin gene
items.explanation: The Gowers maneuver, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a markedly raised creatine kinase suggest Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Most cases carry a deletion or duplication detectable by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification or microarray, so molecular testing is the first step and spares biopsy. Electromyography is nonspecific, and SMN1 testing evaluates spinal muscular atrophy, which does not raise creatine kinase this much.

items.stem: A 6-month-old boy has clusters of sudden flexion of the trunk and arms on waking. His EEG shows hypsarrhythmia, and examination reveals hypopigmented macules. MRI shows cortical tubers. Which treatment has the highest priority, and which adverse effect requires monitoring?
options: Vigabatrin, with monitoring for peripheral visual field constriction
Vigabatrin, with monitoring for bone marrow suppression and anemia
Valproate, with monitoring for hepatic failure and pancreatitis
Adrenocorticotropic hormone, with monitoring for hypertension and infection
items.explanation: Infantile spasms with tuberous sclerosis respond best to vigabatrin, which acts through GABA transaminase inhibition. Permanent peripheral visual field loss is its main toxicity and requires surveillance. Aplastic anemia is a felbamate effect, and hepatotoxicity is a valproate concern in young children. Hormonal therapy is an alternative first-line option but is not preferred in tuberous sclerosis.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has episodes of left hemiparesis and speech arrest that occur while crying hard or blowing on a pinwheel. Angiography shows bilateral terminal internal carotid narrowing with a network of fine collaterals. What mechanism best explains her triggers?
options: Paradoxical cardiac embolism provoked by straining during the crying spell
Vasculitic inflammation worsened by emotional stress
Hypocapnic vasoconstriction reducing flow through stenotic arteries
Arterial dissection from repeated neck strain
items.explanation: Moyamoya disease shows progressive terminal carotid stenosis and a collateral network. Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide, which constricts cerebral vessels and drops perfusion in a tenuous territory, so crying provokes transient ischemic events. Embolism and vasculitis do not explain such reproducible triggers, and dissection would not produce the typical angiographic pattern or bilateral disease. Revascularization surgery such as pial synangiosis is the definitive therapy, and families are taught to avoid hyperventilation triggers and dehydration.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has repeated backward falls, a stiff axial posture, slowed vertical saccades, and a poor response to levodopa. Which MRI finding best supports the diagnosis?
options: Pontine cruciform T2 hyperintensity
Midbrain atrophy with relatively preserved pons
Pulvinar thalamic hyperintensity
Bilateral globus pallidus T2 hyperintensity with a central dark area
items.explanation: Early falls, vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, and levodopa resistance indicate progressive supranuclear palsy. The hummingbird sign of midbrain atrophy supports it. The hot cross bun sign of the pons is typical of multiple system atrophy with cerebellar features, pulvinar signal occurs in variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and the eye of the tiger sign marks pantothenate kinase associated neurodegeneration.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has bilateral visual loss followed by a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning five vertebral segments. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody is positive. Which medication is contraindicated for long-term control?
options: Interferon beta
Rituximab infusions
Azathioprine daily
Inebilizumab infusions
items.explanation: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder with aquaporin-4 antibody differs from multiple sclerosis, and some multiple sclerosis disease-modifying drugs, including interferon beta, fingolimod, and natalizumab, can worsen relapses. Rituximab, azathioprine, and inebilizumab are accepted relapse-prevention agents, as are eculizumab and satralizumab, so these would not be avoided in this disease. Recognizing the antibody target early prevents a harmful drug choice.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment is being considered for an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody. Which feature most increases his risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities?
options: Apolipoprotein E epsilon 2 carrier status
Age under 65 years
Female sex
Apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 homozygosity
items.explanation: Anti-amyloid therapies cause amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or microhemorrhage, and risk is highest in apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 homozygotes, who have the most vascular amyloid. Genotyping is therefore recommended before treatment, together with serial magnetic resonance imaging. Epsilon 2 carriers have lower amyloid burden of the parenchymal type, and age and sex are not the principal determinants.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has delayed speech, hand flapping, and poor eye contact. His mother has mild learning difficulties and a maternal uncle has intellectual disability. Examination shows a long face, prominent ears, and joint hyperextensibility. Which test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
options: Chromosomal microarray for a 15q11 to q13 deletion
DNA testing for FMR1 CGG repeat expansion
Sequencing of MECP2 for loss-of-function variants
Karyotype to detect an extra X chromosome
items.explanation: Intellectual disability, autistic features, macrocephaly with a long face and large ears, and a family history through the maternal line indicate fragile X syndrome, diagnosed by FMR1 repeat expansion testing. A chromosome 15 deletion produces Angelman or Prader-Willi syndrome. MECP2 variants cause Rett syndrome, mostly in girls with regression. An extra X chromosome gives Klinefelter syndrome, which does not fit this picture.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman on lithium for bipolar disorder develops coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, and unsteady gait after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor for hypertension. Which is the most likely mechanism?
options: Inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 metabolism of lithium
Displacement of lithium from albumin binding sites
Reduced renal lithium clearance from lower filtration
Increased intestinal absorption of lithium
items.explanation: Lithium is not metabolized and is excreted almost entirely by the kidneys, so drugs that lower glomerular filtration or promote sodium retention, including ACE inhibitors, thiazides, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, raise levels and cause toxicity. Lithium does not depend on liver enzymes, and it is not protein bound, so displacement and cytochrome inhibition do not explain the rise. Absorption is already nearly complete and is not meaningfully increased.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has several days of severe positional headache that is worse upright and relieved lying flat, with neck stiffness and muffled hearing, 5 days after an epidural for labor. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step if conservative measures fail?
options: Lumbar puncture with removal of 30 mL of cerebrospinal fluid
Intravenous acetazolamide at high dose
Stereotactic occipital nerve block alone
Epidural blood patch
items.explanation: Orthostatic headache after dural puncture indicates cerebrospinal fluid leak with intracranial hypotension. Initial care is fluids, caffeine, and rest, and persistent symptoms respond to an autologous epidural blood patch in most patients. A further lumbar puncture would lower pressure more and worsen the picture. Acetazolamide treats high pressure, not low. An occipital block may reduce pain but does not repair the leak.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has four years of slowly progressive difficulty gripping objects and buckling of the knees. Examination shows weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, with mild dysphagia. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated, and he has not responded to a prednisone trial. Which biopsy finding is most likely?
options: Perifascicular atrophy with perimysial inflammation
Rimmed vacuoles with endomysial inflammatory infiltrates
Scattered necrotic fibers without inflammatory cells
Ragged red fibers with cytochrome oxidase negative fibers
items.explanation: Selective finger flexor and quadriceps weakness in an older man, slow progression, and steroid resistance indicate inclusion body myositis. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and often amyloid or TDP-43 inclusions. Perifascicular atrophy marks dermatomyositis, necrotic fibers without inflammation mark immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, and ragged red fibers suggest mitochondrial myopathy. Inclusion body myositis typically affects finger flexors and quadriceps and responds poorly to immunosuppression, unlike the necrotizing and inflammatory patterns listed here.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy has been seizure free for 4 years on valproate. She plans to conceive in the coming year. Which medication change is the most appropriate?
options: Switch to carbamazepine in the first trimester
Switch to phenytoin before conception
Switch to lamotrigine before conception
Stop all medication and observe closely
items.explanation: Valproate carries the highest risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental harm and should be avoided when possible in women who may become pregnant, so a switch before conception is advised. Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is preferred for generalized epilepsy. Carbamazepine can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures, phenytoin is also teratogenic, and stopping treatment risks recurrence since juvenile myoclonic epilepsy usually relapses.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking an estrogen-containing contraceptive has 5 days of worsening headache, then a focal seizure. Magnetic resonance venography shows thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus, and imaging shows a small hemorrhagic venous infarct. Which management is correct?
options: Full-dose anticoagulation now
Antiplatelet therapy alone
Observation until the hemorrhage resolves
Immediate systemic thrombolysis
items.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation, and a small venous hemorrhagic infarct is not a contraindication because it results from venous congestion, and treatment lowers the risk of further propagation and of venous infarct growth. Antiplatelet therapy is inadequate for venous clot. Delay allows extension of thrombosis. Systemic thrombolysis carries excess bleeding risk and is not standard treatment.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man with genetically confirmed Huntington disease has disabling chorea and starts tetrabenazine. Which adverse effect is most important to counsel about, given the boxed warning?
options: Hepatic failure requiring transplant
Agranulocytosis requiring monitoring
Pulmonary fibrosis with chronic cough
Depression with suicidality
items.explanation: Tetrabenazine and the related vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors deplete presynaptic dopamine and carry a boxed warning for depression and suicidality, a particular concern in Huntington disease where depression is already common. Other effects include sedation, akathisia, and parkinsonism. Liver failure, agranulocytosis, and pulmonary fibrosis are not characteristic of this drug class, so they do not guide counseling.

items.stem: Which patient receiving natalizumab for relapsing multiple sclerosis has the highest estimated risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?
options: Positive antibody, prior immunosuppressant, over 2 years of treatment
Negative antibody status and treatment for 6 months
Positive antibody status without prior immunosuppression, treated 6 months
Negative antibody status with prior immunosuppression, treated 3 years
items.explanation: Three factors stratify risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy on natalizumab: seropositivity for John Cunningham virus antibody, prior immunosuppressant exposure, and treatment duration beyond about 24 months. Risk accumulates when all are present. A patient who is seronegative has a very low risk even with other factors, and short exposure carries low risk, though seronegative patients are retested periodically.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has 2 years of disinhibition, compulsive eating of sweets, and loss of empathy, with preserved memory. His mother developed motor neuron disease in her sixties. Magnetic resonance imaging shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: Trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene
Hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72
Mutation in the presenilin 1 gene
Mutation in the PRNP gene
items.explanation: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia with a family history of motor neuron disease points to the C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion, the most common genetic cause of familial frontotemporal dementia and of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Huntingtin repeats cause Huntington disease with chorea. Presenilin 1 mutations cause early Alzheimer disease with memory loss, and PRNP mutations cause prion disease.

items.stem: A newborn girl has a lumbosacral meningomyelocele repaired on day 2. Her mother had no folate supplementation before conception and has no other risk factors. For the next pregnancy, which preventive measure is recommended?
options: Folic acid 0.4 mg daily only after a positive pregnancy test
Vitamin B12 injections every month throughout pregnancy
Folic acid 4 mg daily from 1 month before conception
A daily multivitamin containing 10,000 units of vitamin A
items.explanation: After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, a much higher folic acid dose is advised, starting before conception and continuing through early pregnancy. The standard low dose is intended for women without a prior affected child and is too small here. Starting after a positive test misses neural tube closure at about 4 weeks. Vitamin B12 alone is not the preventive agent, and excess vitamin A is teratogenic.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has had a normal neurologic examination and negative workup for 2 years of episodes in which her right arm will not move and her voice fails. Symptoms began after her father's death, and she appears unconcerned. Hoover sign is positive. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Tell her the symptoms are imagined and discharge her from care
Explain it as a real functional disorder; refer to physiotherapy
Order repeated brain and spinal imaging until a cause is found
Start an antipsychotic as first-line treatment for the episodes
items.explanation: Positive clinical signs such as the Hoover sign support functional neurological disorder, which should be diagnosed on positive features and explained clearly as real and potentially reversible. Specialized physiotherapy has the best evidence. Dismissing symptoms as imagined damages trust and outcomes. Repeated imaging reinforces illness belief without adding value. Antipsychotics have no role unless a separate psychotic disorder is present.

items.stem: A 44-year-old electrician has had 8 months of slowly progressive weakness of finger extension and grip in the right hand, with visible forearm cramping and fasciculations. Sensation is normal and reflexes in the affected arm are reduced. Nerve conduction studies show motor conduction block in the right ulnar and median nerves outside common entrapment sites, with normal sensory responses. Which treatment is most likely to help?
options: Oral prednisone taper over several months
Riluzole 50 mg twice daily
Intravenous immune globulin
Plasma exchange twice weekly
items.explanation: Asymmetric distal weakness with pure motor involvement and conduction block describes multifocal motor neuropathy, and intravenous immune globulin is the first-line therapy. Corticosteroids are ineffective and may worsen the disorder, unlike in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. Plasma exchange also has little benefit here. Riluzole is used for motor neuron disease, which lacks conduction block and shows upper motor neuron signs.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man in the emergency department continues to have generalized convulsions 20 minutes after receiving two adequate intravenous doses of lorazepam. Which is the most appropriate next medication?
options: Intramuscular haloperidol
Intravenous dexamethasone
Oral topiramate through a nasogastric tube
Intravenous fosphenytoin load
items.explanation: Status epilepticus unresponsive to benzodiazepines requires an urgent second-line antiseizure medication given intravenously, such as fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate, which performed similarly in a large randomized comparison. Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat seizures. Dexamethasone treats vasogenic edema, not status. Oral topiramate absorbs too slowly and unreliably to stop ongoing convulsions, and the time to treatment matters.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man develops sudden left eyelid droop with a dilated left pupil, an eye turned down and out, and right arm and leg weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a small infarct in the left midbrain base. Which vascular territory is involved?
options: Perforators of the proximal posterior cerebral artery
Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Anterior choroidal artery
items.explanation: An ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis is Weber syndrome, caused by infarction of the ventral midbrain where the third nerve fascicle and cerebral peduncle lie together. Perforating branches arising from the basilar apex and proximal posterior cerebral artery supply this region. Lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal infarcts produce capsular syndromes without cranial nerve palsy, and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral pons.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl has had progressive right foot inversion and toe walking for a year. Her symptoms are minimal in the morning and worsen by evening, and her mother has a mild tremor. Which treatment is most likely to give a dramatic and sustained response?
options: Trihexyphenidyl
Botulinum toxin injection
Baclofen
Low-dose levodopa
items.explanation: Childhood-onset leg dystonia with diurnal fluctuation suggests dopa-responsive dystonia, most often from a GTP cyclohydrolase 1 mutation, and it responds markedly and durably to small doses of levodopa without motor fluctuations. Anticholinergics help some dystonias but not reliably or dramatically here. Botulinum toxin and baclofen treat symptoms of other dystonias and do not correct the dopamine deficit.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has painful bilateral visual loss with marked optic disc swelling on fundoscopy. Magnetic resonance imaging shows long segment enhancement of both optic nerves, and the brain is normal. Cerebrospinal fluid lacks oligoclonal bands. Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
options: Aquaporin-4 antibody
Glial fibrillary acidic protein astrocytic antibody
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody
Anti-NMDA receptor antibody
items.explanation: Bilateral optic neuritis with prominent disc edema and long optic nerve involvement, especially in a child, with no oligoclonal bands, favors myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease. Aquaporin-4 antibody tends to cause more severe, posterior or chiasmal involvement in adults. Glial fibrillary acidic protein antibodies cause a meningoencephalomyelitis, and NMDA receptor antibodies cause encephalitis rather than isolated optic neuritis.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has fluctuating alertness, vivid visual hallucinations, and acting out of dreams. She became severely rigid after one dose of haloperidol. Which imaging finding best supports the likely diagnosis?
options: Reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake on SPECT
Selective bilateral hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy
Hot cross bun sign in the pons
Midbrain atrophy with a hummingbird sign
items.explanation: Cognitive fluctuations, well-formed hallucinations, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, and neuroleptic sensitivity define dementia with Lewy bodies, and reduced dopamine transporter uptake on SPECT is a supportive biomarker. Hippocampal atrophy is typical of Alzheimer disease, the hot cross bun sign of multiple system atrophy, and the hummingbird sign of progressive supranuclear palsy, so imaging separates these related dementias.

items.stem: A 14-month-old girl was developing normally until 8 months. She now has loss of purposeful hand use, constant hand wringing, deceleration of head growth, and episodes of breath holding and hyperventilation. Which gene is most likely mutated?
options: UBE3A on chromosome 15
MECP2 on the X chromosome
CDKL5 on the X chromosome
SMN1 on chromosome 5
items.explanation: Normal early development followed by regression, stereotyped hand wringing, acquired microcephaly, and irregular breathing describes classic Rett syndrome in a girl, caused by loss-of-function variants in MECP2 on the X chromosome. UBE3A defects cause Angelman syndrome, with happy demeanor and ataxia. CDKL5 disorder presents with early refractory epilepsy rather than the typical regression pattern. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy with weakness and no cognitive regression.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man who smokes reports 2 months of difficulty rising from a chair, dry mouth, and erectile dysfunction. Examination shows proximal leg weakness, absent ankle reflexes, and reflexes that return briefly after 10 seconds of sustained muscle contraction. Which antibody is most likely to be found?
options: Antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels
Antibody against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Antibody against muscle-specific kinase
Antibody against voltage-gated potassium channel complex
items.explanation: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post-exercise reflex facilitation is the picture of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, caused by antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels, often with small cell lung cancer. Acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific kinase antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which spares reflexes and lacks autonomic features. Potassium channel complex antibodies cause limbic encephalitis or neuromyotonia.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl has daily staring spells of 10 seconds that are provoked by hyperventilation, with generalized 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on electroencephalography. She has also had two generalized tonic-clonic seizures this year. Which drug treats both seizure types?
options: Ethosuximide
Valproate
Carbamazepine
Gabapentin
items.explanation: Childhood absence epilepsy accompanied by generalized tonic-clonic seizures calls for a broad spectrum agent, and valproate controls both seizure types, with lamotrigine as an alternative. Ethosuximide is highly effective for absence alone but does not protect against tonic-clonic seizures.
